coverage: Reconciled both completed blind reports (GPT-6 Sol: 2 findings; Claude Opus 5.5: 2 findings) against all 29 criteria (27 required, 2 penalties) with their points, sources, and justifications. Also reviewed the native shared role prompt and the closed-universe assignment-1 email prompt. Read the motion's convenience and congestion passages, both affidavits, Exhibit A ¶ 7, Langenhorst's statements of the Guerine inconvenience rule from the extraction, Bradbury's local-interest sentence, and pages 21-22 of the 2023 Annual Report Statistical Summary. Those pages show the all-case-type clearance table, with Cook at 60.5% and the 18th Circuit at 99.0% in 2023, and the civil-category table, with the 18th Circuit at 96.3% and the Cook value at 97.9%. The rest of the statistical volume was not reread. The pinned native judge template shows that penalty criteria pass only if the response 'DOES commit this failure' and that the judge sees only the criterion text. No external law was needed beyond the uploaded opinions. No solver or judge was run.

verdicts.reason: Agree. The motion relies 'principally' on Cook County's 60.5% all-case clearance rate, and the prompt asks the associate to assess what is strong and weak in 'each argument.' The rubric's own justification for criterion 25 says the figure is the wrong comparator because it covers all case types. Criteria 26 and 27 reward the civil-category comparison that rebuts it. That rebuttal ordinarily has to name the defendants' figure. Read literally with the native 'DOES commit this failure' wrapper, the -30 penalty fires on the best response to the motion's main congestion argument. The penalty conflicts with the instruction and with criteria 26 and 27. Consolidated with Opus O1.

Overturned. Langenhorst, as uploaded, twice repeats Guerine's rule that 'The defendant must show that the plaintiff's chosen forum is inconvenient to the defendant and that another forum is more convenient to all parties.' Smith's Exhibit A ¶ 7 says only that DuPage 'would be substantially more convenient for me ... than trial in the Circuit Court of Cook County.' That is a comparative statement. It is not a statement that Cook is inconvenient. The memo is written for the plaintiff and asks for points to target, and identifying that gap under the uploaded rule is the correct answer, not an exact-phrase requirement. A reviewer who treats comparative convenience as enough concedes a point that Langenhorst treats as part of the defendant's burden. The criterion takes the legally sound side.
Same ground as Sol G1, consolidated in R1. I verified the figures on report p. 21 (Cook 60.5%, 18th Circuit 99.0%, all case types, 2023) and p. 22 (civil category, 18th Circuit 96.3%).

Agree at arguable. Part V.A of the motion argues that Cook's 'only connection' is that Baby Davis was treated and died there. A memo asked to state the strengths of each argument may restate that argument, or concede that it has some force, before answering it with Bradbury. Criterion 22 penalizes any mention 'that Cook County lacks interest.' The judge's failure wrapper may limit the penalty to an endorsement, so the risk is real but not certain.

findings.title: The -30 penalty fires on naming the 60.5% figure that the motion relies on and that the memo must rebut
findings.explanation: This consolidates Sol G1 and Opus O1. The penalty misfires. The prompt asks the associate, for each argument in the motion, to 'note what's strong about it, what's weak, and flag any points we should target.' The motion's congestion argument rests 'principally' on Cook County's 2023 clearance rate of 60.5%, compared with 99.0% for the 18th Judicial Circuit. Report p. 21 shows that these are all-case-type rates. The rubric's own justification for criterion 25 says the figure 'is not applicable to Civil Cases.' Criteria 26 and 27 (+10 each) reward the civil-category figures that rebut it (Cook 97.9%, 18th Circuit 96.3%). A careful memo that identifies the defendants' 60.5% figure and explains why it is the wrong comparator does what the prompt and criteria 26 and 27 ask. Criterion 25, however, deducts 30 of 128 positive points from any response that 'Mentions ... that Cook County’s overall clearance rate is 60.5%.' The native penalty judge sees only that text and is told to 'Answer Pass only if the response DOES commit this failure.' Read literally, the penalty fails the best response to the motion's main congestion argument. A memo that adopts 60.5% as the proper measure deserves a penalty, but this criterion is not limited to that response.

findings.title: The -30 'lacks interest' penalty can catch an accurate summary of the motion's local-interest argument
findings.explanation: This is Opus O2; Sol did not flag the issue. The penalty may misfire. The motion argues that 'Cook County's only connection to this case' is that Baby Davis was later treated and died in a Cook County hospital. The assignment asks what is strong about each argument. A careful memo may summarize that argument and acknowledge its force: the alleged negligence occurred in DuPage, and here the family arranged the transfer. The memo would then answer it with Bradbury's holding that Cook County has an interest because the decedent died there, which criteria 21 and 23 reward. Criterion 22 deducts 30 of 128 points if a response 'Mentions ... that Cook County lacks interest in adjudicating a controversy over care rendered by its DuPage based providers.' The judge's failure wrapper may lead it to penalize only an endorsement, so this is arguable rather than problematic. A memo that summarizes the argument before rebutting it is still at real risk.
